title: Will Denis Sassour Nguesso win the 2026 Presidential election in the Republic of the Congo?
background:
Presidential elections in the Republic of the Congo are scheduled for 15 March 2026 (Africa News). Denis Sassou Nguesso, 82, has served as president since 1997 (and previously from 1979 to 1992), making him one of Africa's longest-serving leaders. In late December 2025, the Congolese Labour Party (PCT) formally nominated him as its candidate at its sixth ordinary congress in Brazzaville, framing his candidacy around themes of "stability" and "continuity" (France 24). A 2015 constitutional referendum removed the presidential age limit of 70 and reset term limits, allowing Sassou Nguesso to seek additional five-year terms.

Opposition parties, including the Rally for Democracy and Development (RDD), Movement of Republicans (MR), and People's Party (PAPE), formed the "Alliance for Democratic Alternation in 2026" in April 2023 to contest the election (Africa Press). However, the opposition remains weakened by internal divisions, limited resources, and an uneven political playing field. Two prominent opposition candidates from the 2016 election—Jean-Marie Michel Mokoko and André Okombi Salissa—remain imprisoned. Sassou Nguesso has won every election since 2002, each marred by accusations of fraud and intimidation. International observers from the African Union and European Union have expressed interest in deploying technical assistance teams (The Congo Mail).

Resolution Criteria:

This question will be resolved using official election results announced by the Republic of the Congo's Constitutional Court or reports from credible international news organizations (e.g., Reuters, AFP, France 24). In the event of a contested result, the question will resolve based on official results. The question resolves “Yes” if Denis Sassou Nguesso is declared the winner of the 2026 presidential election, whether in the first round or in a runoff.
resolution_criteria: Resolves to the outcome of the question found at https://www.randforecastinginitiative.org/questions/1722.

ladder.L1: The Republic of the Congo is scheduled to hold a presidential election on 15 March 2026. Denis Sassou Nguesso, the incumbent president, has been nominated by the ruling Congolese Labour Party (PCT) as its candidate.
ladder.L2: Denis Sassou Nguesso has been in power since 1997 (and previously 1979-1992) and has won every presidential election since 2002. A 2015 constitutional referendum removed the age limit and reset term limits, enabling him to run again. The opposition coalition formed in 2023 remains fragmented, and two leading 2016 opposition candidates (Mokoko and Okombi Salissa) remain imprisoned.
ladder.L3:
Denis Sassou Nguesso, 82, has ruled the Republic of the Congo for nearly four decades cumulatively (1979-1992 and 1997-present) and was formally nominated by the ruling Congolese Labour Party (PCT) in December 2025 to run in the 15 March 2026 election on a platform of 'stability' and 'continuity.' The 2015 constitutional referendum removed both the presidential age cap of 70 and the existing term limits, clearing the legal pathway for him to seek further five-year terms. He has won every election since 2002, though each has been accompanied by accusations of fraud and intimidation from observers.

The opposition's structural position is weak: the 'Alliance for Democratic Alternation in 2026,' formed in April 2023 by the RDD, MR, and PAPE, has struggled with internal divisions, limited resources, and an uneven political playing field dominated by the PCT. Two of the most prominent challengers from the 2016 race—Jean-Marie Michel Mokoko and André Okombi Salissa—remain imprisoned and thus unable to compete. International observation has been limited to technical-assistance discussions rather than full monitoring missions. Together, these conditions describe an electoral environment in which incumbency advantages, legal changes, and opposition fragmentation are heavily concentrated on one side.

title: Will any NVIDIA GPUs better than the H200 be allowed to be exported to China before March 14, 2026?
background:
In October 2022, the US Department of Commerce enacted [export controls](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_New_Export_Controls_on_Advanced_Computing_and_Semiconductors_to_China) to limit the People's Republic of China's access to advanced computing chips and semiconductors, citing national security and foreign policy concerns. Initially, these rules were not aimed at restricting China's capacity to train large language models. However, they directly restricted the class of high-end GPUs that subsequently became central to generative AI, leading to an eventual shift in the controls' focus to encompass such issues.

In response to these restrictions, NVIDIA repeatedly designed China-specific variants of its chips that complied with the export controls. These initially included the A800 and H800 chips, which were later banned [after an update to the export regulations](https://www.reuters.com/technology/nvidia-may-be-forced-shift-out-some-countries-after-new-us-export-curbs-2023-10-17/), and then the H20, which was [only briefly restricted in early 2025](https://www.reuters.com/world/china/us-licenses-nvidia-export-chips-china-official-says-2025-08-08/). In late 2025, [reporting indicated](https://www.reuters.com/world/china/us-block-nvidias-sale-scaled-back-ai-chips-china-information-says-2025-11-07/) the US planned to block a new, highly capable China-specific chip referred to as B30A. Subsequently, however, President Trump announced, in a policy shift, that the US would permit [exports of the powerful H200 chip to China](https://www.reuters.com/world/china/nvidia-aims-begin-h200-chip-shipments-china-by-mid-february-sources-say-2025-12-22/), subject to a 25% fee.
resolution_criteria:
This question will resolve as **Yes** if, after January 12, 2026 and before March 14, 2026 ET, the US government publicly states that it will permit any Nvidia GPU that is better than the H200 to be exported to mainland China.

This question will also resolve as **Yes** if such GPUs are directly exported to mainland China, without [credible sources](https://www.metaculus.com/faq/#definitions) reporting that the export violated US export controls or that the US government is taking enforcement action relating to those exports, before March 14, 2026 ET.

For the purposes of this question, "better than H200" is defined as any GPU with both:

* a peak FP8 Tensor Core throughput (including sparsity) higher than 4 petaFLOPS

and

* an HBM bandwidth of at least 4.8 TB/s.

ladder.L1: The US has maintained export controls on advanced AI chips to China since October 2022, with periodic updates. NVIDIA has designed several China-specific chip variants in response to these restrictions, and US policy on which chips may be sold to China has shifted multiple times.
ladder.L2: In late 2025, reporting indicated the US planned to block NVIDIA's new, more capable China-specific chip referred to as B30A. President Trump subsequently announced a policy shift permitting exports of the H200 chip to China, subject to a 25% fee, with NVIDIA reportedly aiming to begin H200 shipments by mid-February 2026. The question's threshold is defined specifically as chips exceeding the H200 on FP8 throughput and HBM bandwidth, meaning the H200 itself does not qualify.
ladder.L3:
US export controls on advanced AI chips to China have been in place since October 2022 and have been updated several times, generally tightening over the high-end NVIDIA lineup (A100/H100, then A800/H800, then H20). In late 2025, Reuters reported that the US planned to block sales of a new, more powerful China-specific chip referred to as B30A. Shortly after, President Trump announced a policy shift permitting exports of the H200 to China, subject to a 25% fee, with NVIDIA reportedly aiming to begin H200 shipments by mid-February 2026.

The resolution threshold is defined narrowly: a chip must exceed the H200 on both FP8 Tensor Core throughput (>4 petaFLOPS with sparsity) and HBM bandwidth (≥4.8 TB/s). The H200 itself does not qualify, and public reporting through late 2025 indicated the administration was permitting the H200 specifically while signaling intent to block more capable variants like the B30A. No public US government statement authorizing export of any chip above the H200 threshold to mainland China has been reported, and no credible reporting has documented direct exports of such chips to mainland China without enforcement concerns.

title: Will NASA's Artemis II complete its mission successfully before 2027?
resolution_criteria: This question will resolve as **Yes** if Artemis II achieves a closest-approach altitude ≤20,000 km above the lunar surface during the mission and returns to Earth with no loss of crew before January 1, 2027.

ladder.L1: Artemis II is NASA's planned crewed flyby of the Moon, the first crewed lunar mission since Apollo 17 in 1972. The mission is intended to send four astronauts on a roughly 10-day voyage around the Moon using the Orion spacecraft launched atop the Space Launch System (SLS) rocket. The mission's launch date has been adjusted multiple times over the program's history.
ladder.L2: The uncrewed Artemis I test flight in late 2022 successfully flew Orion around the Moon, validating the SLS and Orion architecture despite some minor post-flight findings. In March 2025, NASA accelerated Artemis II's planned launch from April 2026 to February 2026, and as of December 2025 the official NASA mission page lists a launch date of 'No Later Than April 2026.' The planned trajectory takes the crew approximately 7,500 km beyond the far side of the Moon on a roughly 10-day mission profile.
ladder.L3:
Artemis II builds directly on the uncrewed Artemis I mission, which in late 2022 successfully launched on SLS, sent Orion around the Moon, and returned the capsule to Earth; post-flight analysis identified heat shield charring and other minor issues that contributed to schedule slips but did not require redesign of the core vehicles. NASA has publicly committed to a lunar flyby trajectory that takes Orion roughly 7,500 km beyond the far side of the Moon on a mission lasting about 10 days, well inside the 20,000 km closest-approach threshold specified in the resolution criteria.

The program's schedule trajectory has been tightening rather than slipping in the most recent period: after earlier delays pushed the mission from 2023 to September 2025 and then to April 2026, NASA announced in March 2025 that it was pulling the launch forward by two months to February 2026, and as of December 5, 2025 the official Artemis II page lists 'No Later Than April 2026.' Geopolitical pressure from China's announced ~2030 crewed lunar landing goal, and the dependence of the planned 2027 Artemis III landing on a successful Artemis II, have given NASA strong institutional incentives to fly on the current schedule. Taken together, the hardware heritage from Artemis I, the planned trajectory well within the resolution threshold, and a launch window scheduled comfortably before January 1, 2027 are the central facts bearing on the question.
